title: Opening of A Tale of Two Cities
author: Charles Dickens
intro: One sentence, 118 words, built from pairs of opposites. Dickens opens his novel about the French Revolution by saying the era felt like everything at once: best and worst, wise and foolish, hopeful and despairing. The final clause means loud public voices insisted the time had to be described in extremes.
passage: It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness, it was the epoch of belief, it was the epoch of incredulity, it was the season of Light, it was the season of Darkness, it was the spring of hope, it was the winter of despair, we had everything before us, we had nothing before us, we were all going direct to Heaven, we were all going direct the other way — in short, the period was so far like the present period, that some of its noisiest authorities insisted on its being received, for good or for evil, in the superlative degree of comparison only.

annotations.note: STR: The opening antithesis sets the repeated pattern of paired opposites.
STR: The same antithetical construction moves from historical condition to abstract judgment.
WC -> TO: “Epoch” means era or time period. “Incredulity” means disbelief. The formal words make the sentence sound grand, almost too grand.
FIG/STR: Capitalized Light and Darkness turn the contrast into a cosmic symbolic pair.
STR: The repeated pattern compresses into simpler words, varying the pace inside the parallelism.
WC -> TO: "The other way" is a comic euphemism for Hell, undercutting the high rhetoric.
SHIFT: "In short" breaks the long parallel pattern and signals summary.
INF: Dickens says his own time is like the revolutionary period because both are full of contradictions and loud people making extreme claims.
WC -> TO: "Noisiest" undercuts "authorities," making Dickens sound dryly skeptical.

discussion_prompts: Dickens repeats paired opposites, such as “best/worst” and “wisdom/foolishness.” What does the repetition accomplish?
Find the phrase 'in short.' What does it do to the sentence's tone?
Why does Dickens say 'the period was so far like the present period'? What's he claiming about his own time?
The whole sentence is one sentence. Why didn't Dickens break it into ten or twelve sentences? What's gained by keeping it whole?
discussion_answers: The contradictions pile up rather than cancel out. Each pair adds to a growing sense that the era was everything at once. A plain sentence like "It was an era of contradiction" would be a claim about the period; the repetition makes you feel the contradiction.

It signals a summary is coming and undercuts the grand language of the first half with a casual phrase. The tone steps down from formal and grand to more conversational. Dickens is quietly making fun of people who talk only in extremes.

Dickens suggests that 1859, when he is writing, resembles 1789 specifically in contradiction and exaggerated rhetoric. The historical novel is also a warning about the present: read about France to understand England.

Because the era can't be split into pieces — the contradictions exist simultaneously. Breaking it into ten sentences would suggest the eras alternated; one sentence forces them to coexist. The sentence's FORM is the argument.
